D006-D010_h001.question:
I’ve been feeling completely out of control for the past ten months. At first, I was running the factory floor like a machine—taking on extra shifts, barking orders, snapping at anyone who questioned me. Little things set me off—a typo on a report, a late delivery—and I’d explode. I started so many projects I couldn’t even keep track, jumping from one to another, never finishing. But around eight months ago, things got… strange. I began feeling bugs crawling under my skin, like wires being threaded through my arms, even though nothing was there. I told my wife, “The grid is pulsing,” and started calling the monitoring devices “stingtags”—words I just made up, but they made perfect sense to me. I became convinced management was implanting signals in my nervous system, watching my every move.

All that agitation burned out after a while. The last three months, I’ve just stayed in bed. I don’t answer calls, not even from my kids. I catch myself thinking, “Maybe I won’t wake up tomorrow,” and it doesn’t scare me. But those crawling feelings and the paranoia—those never left, even as the rest faded. They started when I was manic and never let go, but I can tell they came *with* the high, not on their own.
D006-D010_h001.options:
A. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
    B. Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder
    C. Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type)
    D. Delusional Disorder
D006-D010_h001.answer: A. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features

D006-D010_h002.question:
I’ve been through a lot over the past year. Ever since my wife passed five years ago, I’ve lived alone, and things really started changing about ten months ago. At first, I felt incredible—like I’d turned back the clock. I was full of energy, couldn’t sit still, and stayed up for days rearranging furniture or walking around the neighborhood at odd hours. My mind raced, and the smallest sounds—a car door closing, a bird chirping—would grab my attention instantly. I felt like people were watching me from across the street, maybe government folks, and sometimes I saw shadows of men in dark suits standing outside my window, though no one was there. I even heard them whispering, but that was later.

My speech must’ve gotten hard to follow—my daughter said I was jumping between ideas, not making sense. That high lasted nearly a year, but three months ago, the energy vanished. I stopped going to my chess club, didn’t care to cook or eat. I filled a bottle with pills one night… but couldn’t go through with it. Now I’m calmer, but those hallucinations and confused thoughts only ever happened during that intense, restless period. When the mania faded, they went with it.
D006-D010_h002.options:
A. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
    B. Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder
    C. Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type)
    D. Delusional Disorder
D006-D010_h002.answer: A. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features

D006-D010_h003.question:
I’ve been really up and down for the past ten months—mostly up, actually. I’d wake up with so much energy, like I could run a marathon or solve every problem at work without breaking a sweat. But I couldn’t focus—charts, prescriptions, even conversations—they’d all blur together. My mind jumps from one thing to the next. I’ve snapped at coworkers for no reason, then minutes later felt on top of the world. And for about eight of those months, I’ve been hearing voices—mostly a man’s voice telling me I’m destined for something greater, that I’m special. I believe he’s a famous cardiologist who’s been watching me, that he’s in love with me and will sweep me away. I know it sounds strange, but the way he speaks—it’s so real.  

But then three months ago, it crashed. I didn’t care about anything—winning Pharmacist of the Year, my achievements… none of it mattered. I stood on the roof of my building once, just feeling this sudden pull to jump. No plan, just… an urge.  

But here’s the thing—the voices? They started with the high and never come when I’m not manic. When the energy drops, the voices fade too.
D006-D010_h003.options:
A. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
    B. Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder
    C. Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type)
    D. Delusional Disorder
D006-D010_h003.answer: A. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features

D006-D010_h004.question:

I also became sure people were sending me secret messages—neighbors coughing in code, TV ads flashing hidden signs meant just for me.

But when the energy crashed three months ago, it was worse. I stopped returning calls, isolated myself. I even worked out how I’d end it—specific, planned. Thank God I didn’t act. 

The smells and delusions only ever happened during that high period. When I’m stable, they vanish. They haven't lingered beyond the mania.

    C. Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type)
    D. Delusional Disorder

D006-D010_h005.question:

D006-D010_h006.question:

But here’s the thing—the voices, the smells, the certainty that it’s all over—they only hit when I’m in this wired-up state. When the high fades, it all goes quiet. I don’t hear it. I don’t smell it.     C. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features

D006-D010_h007.question:

But here’s the thing—none of the voices, none of the sensations, none of that grand feeling happened *before* the mania kicked in. And when I finally crashed, they all went away. They’ve only ever come with the high.
D006-D010_h007.options:
A. Major Depressive Disorder
    B. Bipolar II Disorder
    C. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
    D. Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type)

D006-D010_h022.question:
I’ve been really up and down for the past year and a half. Last spring, I suddenly felt like I could do anything—like I was meant to change the world. I was working on five research papers at once, barely sleeping—sometimes just two hours a night—but I wasn’t tired at all. I maxed out my credit cards buying books, lab supplies, even a laptop I didn’t need. I felt electric, unstoppable.

But then, about three months into that high, things twisted. I started seeing shadows in my apartment—figures standing in corners, watching me. I knew they weren’t real, but I *saw* them. I became convinced the planet was collapsing, that civilization would end in weeks. I stopped talking to friends; why bother, if everything was ending? I’d catch myself rhyming while talking—like “I’m not weak, I seek the peak”—it made no sense, but I couldn’t stop.

After months like that, the energy crashed. I couldn’t get out of bed, spoke so slowly people finished my sentences. I gained over 15 pounds. I’d wake at 4 a.m. every day and just lie there, hollow.

But here’s the thing: the voices and visions, the delusions—they’ve never stayed when I’m not manic. They come with the highs and go when the mania fades. They don’t linger.
D006-D010_h022.options:
A. Binge-Eating Disorder
    B. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
    C. Persistent Depressive Disorder
    D. Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type)
D006-D010_h022.answer: B. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features

D006-D010_h023.question:
I’ve been a PhD researcher in neuroscience for the past four years, and things started unraveling about a year ago. At first, I was hyper-focused—writing papers, applying for grants, teaching, all while sleeping maybe three hours a night and still feeling electric, like I’d had ten coffees. But the ideas started getting… loud. Voices in my head arguing with me, telling me the world was ending, that my research was part of a global conspiracy. I believed them. I’d talk back, sometimes rhyming without meaning to—words just snapping together like it made perfect sense, even when it didn’t.

I maxed out credit cards buying lab equipment I didn’t need, convinced I was on the verge of a breakthrough that could save humanity before the collapse. But when the funding got frozen and my advisor intervened, everything crashed. I withdrew, couldn’t speak without slowing down so much people finished my sentences. I cried all the time, lost over ten pounds, and kept waking up from nightmares where the earth cracked open.

Now the voices are quieter, but I still feel flat—blank. The delusions and hallucinations only ever happened during that intense high period and the immediate crash after. They never stayed once the mania faded, which my doctor said is important—I think he was checking if it was “something else.”
D006-D010_h023.options:
A. Binge-Eating Disorder
    B. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
    C. Persistent Depressive Disorder
    D. Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type)
D006-D010_h023.answer: B. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features

D006-D010_h024.question:
I’m a 49-year-old professor—tenured, married, usually pretty composed. But for about the past year, everything spiraled. At first, I was working nonstop, barely sleeping—three hours a night, sometimes none. I felt razor-sharp, like I didn’t need rest. I’d call colleagues at 3 a.m., organize wild department events, even tried driving to a conference in another state without a plan. My wife said I was agitated, always pacing, snapping over little things.

During that time, I became convinced she was seeing someone—saw shadows of men in our home, even “saw” her meeting someone at the campus library. I tried explaining it to her, but I know my words didn’t make sense—I was jumping from idea to idea, losing track. That’s when the visual hallucinations started: figures in the periphery, disappearing when I turned.

Now the mania’s faded, and I’ve crashed—low mood, can’t get out of bed, gained weight. I feel slow, like I’m wading through mud. But the delusions and hallucinations? They only happened during that high period. They stopped when the mania did.
D006-D010_h024.options:
A. Binge-Eating Disorder
    B. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
    C. Persistent Depressive Disorder
    D. Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type)
D006-D010_h024.answer: B. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features

D006-D010_h025.question:
I’ve been struggling for over a year now—work’s hard, my wife’s worried, and I just can’t keep things together. About a year ago, I suddenly felt on top of the world. I was full of energy, barely sleeping—like four hours and I was wide awake, itching to go. I’d weld extra jobs, start renovations at home, call people in the middle of the night to hang out. I wasn’t reckless? Nah—I drove like a maniac once or twice, took some pills at a party, things I’d never do sober. I felt bulletproof.

But during that time, things got… weird. I became convinced my organs were rotting—doctors say I’m fine, but I *felt* it. Like bugs crawling under my skin, even now sometimes. I’d say things like “I’m a spark in the dark, lighting the lark,” just because it sounded sharp—my wife said I wasn’t making sense. I stopped calling friends, didn’t want the noise—they couldn’t understand.

When that high crashed, I flattened out. Started crying over nothing. Couldn’t eat. Took forever to fall asleep. Even lifting a wrench felt heavy. That lasted months. But the key thing? The bugs, the rhyming, the body beliefs—they *only* came during that crazy high spell. Never before, never since.
D006-D010_h025.options:
A. Binge-Eating Disorder
    B. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
    C. Persistent Depressive Disorder
    D. Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type)
D006-D010_h025.answer: B. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
